questions.q: What kind of scenario is the Prairiewind Underwriters case study in this lesson?
options: A real, named incident at an actual insurance company
An illustrative, fictional, composite scenario built to teach a real failure pattern
A hypothetical that never actually involves a production outage
A direct continuation of Harlow Creek Logistics under a different name
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that Prairiewind is fictional and illustrative, not a real company or a real reported incident.

questions.q: What did Prairiewind's application databases actually do during the regional outage?
options: They failed over to the secondary region exactly within their documented RTO
They were destroyed and had to be rebuilt from backups
They never attempted to fail over at all
They failed over, but to the wrong region entirely
questions.explain: Both the claims and quoting databases failed over correctly and on schedule -- the application-tier DR plan worked exactly as designed.

questions.q: What was the actual root cause of Prairiewind's extended outage?
options: The claims database's data was corrupted during failover
The review board's cost projections were inaccurate
The shared hub -- firewall, gateway, DNS resolver -- was never deployed to the secondary region, so failed-over spokes had no working network
The quoting application had a software bug unrelated to infrastructure
questions.explain: Every spoke depended on the hub for egress and DNS, and the hub itself had no secondary-region deployment or documented RTO/RPO.

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT one of the three contributing factors the lesson identifies for why the review board missed the gap?
options: The review checklist was shaped around application-tier RTO/RPO
Ownership of the hub's DR plan was ambiguous between Platform and application teams
The architecture diagram's symmetry implied the secondary region was fully built out
The review board was never shown a network diagram of any kind
questions.explain: Prairiewind's review board did see diagrams and detailed application-tier numbers -- the gap was a category of risk never on the checklist, not a lack of material.

questions.q: What single question, if asked during either review session, would have surfaced Prairiewind's gap?
options: What is the total headcount of the platform team?
If the primary region's hub goes down, what happens to every spoke that depends on it, and is that dependency's RTO/RPO documented?
How many tags does each subscription currently have?
What programming language was the quoting application written in?
questions.explain: That question forces the shared-services tier onto the same RTO/RPO checklist as every application tier -- exactly the gap ADR-003 closes in Lesson 30's design.
